newsitem.title: USA: FBI probe Olympic bombing interrogation methods.
newsitem.headline: FBI probe Olympic bombing interrogation methods.

text.p: FBI Director Louis Freeh said on Tuesday his agency was conducting two internal inquiries involving the Olympics bombing and former security guard Richard Jewell, who has been cleared as suspect.
Freeh said the FBI began an inquiry late last month into Jewell's interrogation and the "propriety" of the manner in which FBI agents questioned him.
Another inquiry into leaks to the media that Jewell was a suspect was launched immediately after stories naming Jewell appeared.
Both inquiries, conducted by the FBI's Office of Professional Responsibility and involving possible improper conduct by FBI employees, are "ongoing," Freeh said in a two-page statement.

On July 30, after he had been named in the news accounts, two FBI agents went to Jewell's apartment and asked him to come to the FBI's office in Atlanta to help make a training film on how to question a witness.

During the videotaped session, one FBI agent told Jewell, a former security guard, that he wanted the film to be realistic and asked him to sign a waiver of his constitutional rights to remain silent and to have a lawyer present.

As Jewell was handed the waiver form, he became concerned and asked to call a lawyer. His attorneys have said the FBI used the training film as a ruse in an attempt to get a videotaped statement that Jewell had waived his rights.

Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick said she learned about the incident three or four weeks ago and expressed concern. "I don't like it," she said, adding that such tactics may jeopardise later prosecutions.

Jewell on Saturday was notified by a U.S. Justice Department prosecutor that he no longer was a target in the investigation into the July 27 bombing at Atlanta's Centennial Olympic Park. Two people died as a result of the blast and more than 100 were injured.
Attorneys for Jewell have vowed to sue the news organisations that first named him as a suspect, and also are considering legal action against the federal government
They have blamed Jewell's ordeal on Freeh, saying the entire case against him was directed by senior FBI officials.
Freeh in his statement did not apologise to Jewell and made no mention that he had been cleared. But he did sternly warn FBI employees that leaks would not be tolerated.
"The federal, state and local investigators assigned to the Olympic bombing investigation have worked tirelessly to pursue all leads and potential suspects," Freeh said.
"It is important to keep in mind that complex investigations such as this often require a long-term commitment of resources to solve such a heinous crime," he said.
Freeh said the internal inquiries were being overseen by the Justice Department.
